item.title: Omizutori: The Fire and Water Rites of Todaiji — Guide
item.description: Omizutori is the popular name for Shuni-e, a series of sacred Buddhist rites held at Todaiji’s Nigatsudo hall over the first two weeks of March, and one of Japan’s oldest ceremonies — performed every year without interruption since 752, over 1,270 years. Its most spectacular moment is the Otaimatsu each evening, when monks race along the hall’s wooden veranda swinging enormous flaming pine torches, showering embers over the crowd gathered below (sparks are said to bring good luck and blessing).

item.title: Wakakusa Yamayaki: Nara's Mountain-Burning Fire Festival — Guide
item.description: The Wakakusa Yamayaki, held on the fourth Saturday of January, is one of Nara’s oldest and most spectacular festivals: after nightfall, the entire dry grassy dome of Mount Wakakusa behind Nara Park is deliberately set on fire, its whole slope glowing red and orange against the winter dark. The blaze is preceded by a large fireworks display over the hill, making a rare and dramatic combination of fireworks and mountain fire.

item.title: Nozawa Onsen Dosojin Fire Festival: One of Japan's Great Fire Festivals — Guide
item.description: The Nozawa Onsen Dosojin Fire Festival, held every 15 January, is considered one of Japan’s three great fire festivals, a dramatic and intense nighttime spectacle centred on a huge wooden shrine (shaden) built by the villagers. In the festival’s climax, men aged 25 and 42 (considered unlucky ages) defend the structure from villagers attacking with flaming torches in a fierce battle of fire, before the shrine is finally set alight, all as a prayer for a good harvest, family wellbeing and the blessing of children, set against the deep snow of the mountain village.
